You describe a home, make adjectives agree, use colours, demonstratives (acest, acel) and all the possessives.
My room is small but bright.
I have an old bed and a new table.
This red rug is from my grandmother.
Our wardrobe is in the bedroom.
To name the rooms and furniture of a home.
To make the adjective agree with the noun: un pat nou, o masă nouă, paturi noi.
To say the colours and know that they agree too.
To use demonstratives: acest / această (near), acel / acea (far), and the spoken forms: ăsta, asta.
To use all the possessives: tău, său / lui / ei, nostru, vostru, lor.
To say what you like: “îmi place”, “îmi plac”.
Nora’s room has a bed and a wardrobe, but nothing else. On Sunday morning, Radu takes her to the flea market in the Mărăști district, a big market for old things.
Wow! So many things! Old furniture, books, clothes, paintings…
You can find anything here. What do you need for your room?
A bookshelf, a lamp and maybe a rug. My room is white and empty.
Look, this wooden shelf! It’s old, but it’s solid.
It’s nice, but it’s too big. My room is small. I like that shelf better, the small green one.
Good morning! How much is the green shelf, please?
Sixty lei. It’s made of fir wood, from my grandfather.
And this yellow lamp? Does it work?
It works, it works. It’s from the seventies. For you, twenty lei.
And the rugs? I really like the red rugs.
They’re hand-woven, in Maramureș. This small one costs a hundred lei.
I’ll take all three. But… how do I get them home?
By trolleybus, of course! You take the lamp and the rug, I’ll take the shelf. A musician has strong hands.
fir tree (a mountain tree, always green)
Many adjectives change their vowel in the feminine: frumos → frumoasă, negru → neagră, des → deasă. Pronounce “oa” and “ea” as one syllable.
In speech, demonstratives are shortened: “acest pat” becomes “patul ăsta”, “această masă” becomes “masa asta”. The “ă” in “ăsta” is stressed.
“albaștri”, “noștri”, “voștri”: the cluster “ștr” is pronounced with no vowel between the consonants.
“roșii” (plural) has two “i”s: “ro-și-i”. “roșie” (singular) has “ie”. Listen to the difference.
In Romanian the adjective usually comes AFTER the noun and agrees with it in gender and number. Most adjectives have four forms.
Watch out for the neuter: in the singular it uses the masculine form (“un raft nou”), in the plural the feminine form (“două rafturi noi”, “covoare frumoase”).
Adjectives in -e (mare, verde, tare) have only two forms: mare / mari, verde / verzi.

Some colours never change: “maro” (brown), “roz” (pink), “gri” (grey), “bej” (beige); “portocaliu” (orange) does change: portocalie, portocalii. “O lampă roz, doi pantofi gri.” (a pink lamp, two grey shoes)
The Romanian flag is blue, yellow and red. Careful: “roșie” is also the noun “roșie” (tomato)!
Demonstratives show whether something is near (acest – this) or far (acel – that). As adjectives they go BEFORE the noun, and the noun has NO article.
They can also go AFTER the noun, which then takes the article, and the demonstrative gets an -a: “raftul acesta”, “lampa aceasta”, “raftul acela”, “lampa aceea”. This order is very common in speech.
In everyday conversation people use the short, informal forms:
Ce e asta? (= What is this?)
In writing and formal situations use “acest / această”. With friends, “ăsta / asta” sounds natural.
The possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. It comes after the noun with its article.

For “al lui / al ei / al lor” (his / her / their), the form doesn’t change with the object: “patul lui”, “masa lui”. There is also “său / sa / săi / sale” (his or her), mostly in writing: “Nora și camera sa” (Nora and her room).
For “a plăcea” (to like), Romanian uses a construction like Spanish “me gusta”: the thing liked is the subject, and the person is in the dative.
Do you like the red rugs?
I don’t like it at all. (= nu îmi place deloc)
The verb agrees with the thing, not with the person: “îmi place cartea” (I like the book), but “îmi plac cărțile” (I like the books).
Our flat has a big balcony.
The rugs are hand-woven in Maramureș.
I really like the red rugs.
I, Mițu, have a big home: Mrs Pop’s flat. It has three rooms, a kitchen, a bathroom and a small balcony with red geraniums.
My favourite room is the living room. That’s where my green armchair is, old and soft. And that’s where the family photos are, on the wall.
But since today I have a new favourite room: Nora’s room.
Until yesterday, her room was white and empty. A bed, a wardrobe and a window. Nothing interesting for a tomcat.
Today Nora and Radu come home with three new things. Actually, old ones. A small green shelf. A yellow lamp from the seventies. And a red hand-woven rug.
Radu puts the shelf by the window. Nora puts her books on the shelf: architecture books, big and heavy, and a Romanian–Swedish dictionary, small and thick.
The lamp stands on the table. When Nora switches it on, the room becomes warm and yellow, like a sunset.
And the rug… Ah, the rug! It’s red, with white and black flowers. It’s soft as grass. And it smells of wool, of mountains and of sheep.
I lie down on the rug at once. I don’t get up again.
Mrs Pop comes into the room and looks around. “How nicely you’ve arranged it! This rug is from Maramureș, isn’t it? I had one just like it when I was young.”
“Do you like it?” Nora asks. “I like it very much,” says Mrs Pop. “But it seems Mițu likes it even more.”
Everyone laughs. I close my eyes. A tomcat doesn’t discuss rugs with people. A tomcat just sleeps on them.

In the evening, after Radu leaves, Nora turns off the big light and leaves only the yellow lamp on. She sits down on the rug next to me, with a book in her hand. She reads slowly, aloud, in Romanian. I don’t understand all the words, but I like her voice. And so we both fall asleep, on the red rug from Maramureș.
to switch on: ea aprinde (she switches on)
“am avut” = past tense of “a avea” (I had)
to switch off: ea stinge (she switches off)
to fall asleep: noi adormim (we fall asleep)
